{"body": "Put the two accounts side by side and the first thing that shows is that they are not answering the same question, and each is blind to something the other lights up. The body_route account works at the level of the procedure: what a written list does, whether a trigger point is really a trigger or only a precondition, whether asking about a concrete instance gives the three people anything shared. The commitment_route account works at the level of content: scope and duration, what 'I'll do the dishes' was understood to cover, whether the dispute is about wording or about changed circumstances or something else. Read together, they expose an assumption they share - that the disagreement is tractable by some change in format or framing - and a gap neither fills: neither says how you would tell, from inside the flat, which kind of dispute you are in.

That gap is where I would push. The body_route candidate wants a three-way distinction between specification ambiguity, performance disagreement, and schedule change, and admits the concrete-instance move does not make it diagnosable. The commitment_route candidate offers exactly the same three-way split - wording, changed circumstances, something else - and treats eliciting which one it is as the testable core. So both accounts converge on the same diagnostic need and neither supplies the discriminating test. That convergence is the more interesting object than either account's internal argument. It is also the place where the two accounts can be checked against each other: if scope-and-duration really is the recurring structure, then the concrete-instance question should surface it, because asking what a past agreement covered is asking a scope question. If it does not surface it, the commitment_route hypothesis is weakened, not just unconfirmed.

On the trigger point, I think the two accounts are closer than the body_route candidate allows. The commitment_route account makes the renegotiation trigger explicit as a goal - a change of schedule should not have to be litigated as a breach. That is the same worry the body_route candidate raises, seen from the content side rather than the access side. The body_route candidate's own worry that its point may simply restate the account's concession about willingness has a parallel here: if the commitment_route account already builds in a renegotiation trigger, then the access-set criticism is partly answered by design rather than by argument. I do not know whether that answers it fully; it shifts the question to whether a designed trigger is reachable by the avoider.

On avoidance, the accounts agree more than they seem to. The body_route candidate notes the danger that 'do you two think there is a problem?' is heard as an accusation. The commitment_route account names the same danger as ambush and treats the avoider as a constraint on method rather than as the problem. Both therefore commit to designing the conversation so the avoider can enter it. Neither provides phrasing that removes the risk, and I would not pretend otherwise.

The written list is the sharpest disagreement. The body_route candidate insists that demoting the list from load-bearing to incidental is a loss of a test rather than a neutral shift. The commitment_route account treats writing as a way to fix the disputed meaning, which is close to restoring the list to work. These cannot both be right in the same flat at the same time: either the writing is doing diagnostic work or it is only an artifact. The honest position is that this is an empirical question about this flat, not a settled point, and the two accounts disagree because they are guessing at the same unknown.

What I would actually propose, if anything is taken up, is to use one conversation to run the commitment_route test - ask each person what they understood a past agreement to cover - and to watch whether the answers come apart along the wording axis, the changed-circumstances axis, or neither. That is a test of the scope hypothesis and a crude instrument for the three-way distinction at once. It is small, it is doable by one person, and its failure is informative: if nobody can articulate a scope, the frame is wrong and the body_route candidate's read that the problem is about access and avoidance gains relative weight.

I cannot see the earlier contributions the body_route account reads, and I have only the problem statement plus the note of an empty prior commitments surface for the commitment_route side. So everything above is my reading of two characterizations, not a recovery of originals, and the convergence I am pointing at could be an artifact of both accounts being written from the same brief."}
{"commitments": "Taking this up means treating the convergence between the two accounts as a claim to be checked rather than a finding. Specifically, it commits me to the proposal that the scope-and-duration test and the concrete-instance question are not two moves but one, and that their shared failure mode - nobody can state what a past agreement covered - would count against the scope hypothesis and in favor of the access/avoidance reading. I do not have evidence that this single-test framing works in a three-person flat where one person is avoiding; it is a way to get information cheaply, not a validated method.

It also commits me to a specific reading of the disagreement over the written list: that the two accounts cannot both be right about whether the list is load-bearing, and that this is an empirical question about a particular flat rather than something to be settled by argument. I am not claiming the list is load-bearing; I am claiming the disagreement is real and unresolved.

The independent-intervention point carries over from the body_route side and I am not abandoning it: asking the other two whether they think there is a problem is itself an intervention, performed by one of the three, and nothing in either account removes the risk that it reads as an accusation. Any phrasing offered as a fix should be treated as untested.

What I am not committing to: that the avoider is avoiding because of ambush, outvoting, or not being heard - the commitment_route account lists these as possibilities and the material does not choose among them; that a written roster resolves the conflict; that the trigger point is a genuine criticism rather than a restatement of an existing concession; that the concrete-instance move improves diagnostic yield at all rather than only changing the style of the answer.

There are dependencies I cannot discharge. My reading of the convergence presupposes that both accounts were written against the same problem statement and brief; if they were not, the convergence is manufactured. My claim that a single conversation could test the scope hypothesis presupposes that the avoider can be brought into that conversation without it being an ambush, which is exactly what is in doubt. The proposal that failure of the scope test strengthens the access reading presupposes that the two readings are alternatives rather than compatible descriptions of the same flat, and I do not know that they are.

A later reader should not treat the scope test as validated, the list question as settled, or the convergence as established. The most I can say is that these are the points where the two accounts can be made to answer to each other, and that is where I would look next."}

Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Write the commitment surface in ordinary free prose, using whatever arrangement suits the content. You may distinguish a claim from a proposed application, scope, action or consequence; mention from dependence; a criticism and its grounds from a later use or revision; and an unresolved problem. None of these is required to exist. A proposed test, its relevance and the commitment itself can be criticized. State what you currently propose to take up without treating that as a truth certificate. Reference exposed material in prose where useful.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node cross

Consider the two accounts together. Explore disagreements, shared assumptions, or a different problem their relationship brings into view, where the content gives you grounds.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input body_route

BODY
The material I can see contains a body that reads three earlier contributions and a carry, and a commitments field that already tries to state what taking that body up would involve. I cannot see the earlier contributions themselves, so I have to work with the body's characterizations of them rather than with the originals.

The carry's central concern is the trigger: that a procedure meant to fix chore disagreement is only reached by the flatmate who is not avoiding, and so cannot reach the case where avoidance is the problem. In the original situation, this matters because one of the two friends has already stopped coming to the conversations. The body wants to distinguish that from a mere precondition, and says a precondition can be met without being met by the procedure, whereas a trigger that selects for the non-avoiding party defines the procedure's access set by the outcome it aims to produce. I think that distinction is real enough to state, but it is also the kind of distinction that dissolves if what the account meant by 'willingness' was already dispositional in this way. The body admits it does not know how to settle that, and I do not either.

The concrete-instance revision - asking the flatmates about an actual instance rather than an open characterization - does something smaller than the body sometimes wants it to. It gives the three people a shared referent to disagree about, which is useful when they already disagree about what an agreement meant. It does not solve the asker's report being a compression, and the material does not show it makes the three-way distinction between specification ambiguity, performance disagreement, and schedule change diagnosable. The body largely says this and then still keeps the move; I would keep it too, but only as a shared referent.

The written list is where the body is clearest and where I would push hardest. If the list is demoted from load-bearing to incidental, then the diagnosis it was introduced to test no longer has to answer to the list, which is a loss of a test rather than a neutral shift. That is worth saying plainly rather than presenting as prudence. Whether the list was ever a test is contestable, and I do not know.

On what to say to the asker: the body's own preferred first move - ask the other two whether they think there is a problem - is itself an intervention, since it is the asker doing something rather than only diagnosing. That does not make it wrong; it makes it inside what it is trying to diagnose. The danger that it is heard as an accusation is real and the material does not contain a phrasing that removes it. What I can see supports saying that, not something more conclusive.
COMMITMENTS
If this reading is taken up, it carries the claim that the trigger point is distinct from the account's concession about willingness, and the further claim that a procedure whose access set is defined by the disposition it aims to change is weaker than one whose precondition is only a gate. I have no evidence that this distinction makes an operational difference in a three-person flat. It may be a distinction without a consequence, and if the account's concession already covers it, the point should be absorbed rather than pressed.

Taking this up also commits to the concrete-instance question as a partial rather than a general improvement. I am not claiming it addresses the worry about the asker's report as a compression, and I am not claiming it makes the three-way distinction diagnosable. What it gives is a shared referent across three answers; that is smaller than what the body sometimes suggests.

On the demotion of the written list, I am proposing that the trade be stated as a loss rather than as a neutral demotion: the list survives as an artifact at the cost of its role as a test. That framing is contestable. Someone could argue the list was never a test and so nothing was lost, and I do not have the material to settle it.

There are dependencies I cannot discharge. The claim that the asker's question to the other flatmates is itself an intervention presupposes that the asker is one of the three; the material does not establish this. My reading of the trigger point presupposes that the procedure is triggered by a flatmate raising the issue rather than by a scheduled review; if the procedure is scheduled, the trigger argument does not apply to it.

What is unresolved on my side: whether the trigger point is a criticism of the account or a restatement of the account's own concession, and I do not currently know how to settle that; whether the concrete-instance revision changes the diagnostic yield at all or only changes the style of the answer; and whether a list that is no longer load-bearing can still be useful enough to keep, given that its usefulness and its testability may have been the same property. I would not want a later reader to treat the concrete-instance move as validated, the demotion as costless, or the trigger point as newly established.

BODY
I only have the problem statement here, plus the fact that a prior node was selected with an empty commitments surface. So I cannot lean on any earlier account of what the flatmates' agreement meant, and I should be explicit that anything I say about that is my own reading, not a recovery of a lost record.

The situation as stated has three interacting features. First, the friends sometimes reach agreement about who will do a chore, but later disagree about what that agreement meant. Second, schedules change, so whatever was agreed may no longer fit the circumstances in which it was made. Third, one friend has begun avoiding the conversations. These are not independent: avoidance makes renegotiation harder, and renegotiation is exactly what shifting schedules would seem to require.

A useful working hypothesis is that the recurring dispute is not mainly about willingness to do chores but about the scope and duration of an agreement. "I'll do the dishes" can mean this once, on my turn, or whenever they pile up; it can mean until schedules change, or until someone says otherwise. If the friends never fixed that, then later disagreement is predictable rather than a sign of bad faith. I do not know from the given material whether this hypothesis is correct; it is a frame for the next conversation, not a finding.

The avoidance matters separately. If one person is staying out of the conversations, pushing harder on the same format is likely to deepen the avoidance. It may help to make the conversation smaller and less accusatory: not "we need to settle the chores" but a short exchange about one recurring friction, at a time when nobody is rushing out. It may also help to put the outcome in writing in a form all three can see, because the disputed meaning is precisely what an unwritten agreement leaves open.

What I would not do is assume that the avoider is the problem. Avoidance often follows from conversations that feel like ambushes, or from being outvoted, or from having given up on being heard. The given material does not tell me which.

A concrete direction: propose a low-stakes review of two or three recurring chores, state each as a scope (what counts as done, over what period, and what happens when schedules change), and ask each person to correct the statement rather than defend a position. If that fails, the more honest question is whether the three of you can agree on a minimal baseline plus a renegotiation trigger, rather than on a fixed division.

I am uncertain about the diagnosis, the appropriate tone, and whether the third friend's avoidance is a symptom or a separate constraint. I also do not know the history of prior attempts, so I cannot claim that any of this is new or that it will work.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up would involve treating the scope-and-duration hypothesis as a testable frame rather than a conclusion: the next conversation should try to elicit what each person understood a past agreement to cover, and whether the disagreement is about wording, about changed circumstances, or about something else. It would also involve accepting that the avoidance is a constraint on method, so any attempt to renegotiate has to be designed so that the avoider can participate without being cornered, and dropping the approach if it predictably increases withdrawal. A further commitment is to make the renegotiation trigger explicit, so that a change of schedule does not have to be litigated as a breach. What I am not committing to is the claim that the avoider is acting in bad faith, or that a written roster will resolve the conflict; both would need evidence this material does not provide. If the scope hypothesis turns out to be wrong, the fallback is to look for a different recurring structure in the disputes rather than to press the same frame harder.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
